questions.question: When did Voyager 1 enter interstellar space?
questions.no_rag: Voyager 1 left the Solar System in 2013, becoming the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.
questions.no_rag_note: Mixes up NASA's 2013 announcement with the 2012 crossing, and gives no source to check.

claims.text: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause and entered interstellar space on August 25, 2012, the first spacecraft ever to do so.
As of August 2026 it is about 171 AU from Earth, the most distant human-made object.

questions.question: Why was the Apollo 13 Moon landing aborted?
questions.no_rag: Apollo 13's landing was cancelled because of an explosion on board ("Houston, we've had a problem"). The crew looped around the Moon and returned safely.
questions.no_rag_note: Broadly right but vague, with no cause and no findings. Nothing in it can be traced to a source.

claims.text: The landing was aborted after an oxygen tank in the service module exploded two days into the mission, disabling its electrical and life-support system.
A routine stir of the tank ignited damaged wire insulation inside it, and the explosion vented both of the service module's oxygen tanks to space.
An investigative review board later found fault with the preflight testing of the oxygen tank and with Teflon being placed inside it.

questions.question: What did Margaret Hamilton contribute to the Apollo program?
questions.no_rag: Margaret Hamilton wrote the software for the Apollo missions and is credited with coining the term "software engineering".
questions.no_rag_note: Correct, but a reader cannot verify it. Even when the model already knows the answer, RAG adds traceability.

claims.text: Margaret Hamilton directed the Software Engineering Division at the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory and led the development of the on-board flight software for the Apollo Guidance Computer.
She coined the term "software engineering" to give software the same standing as other engineering disciplines.
In 2016 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom for that work.

questions.question: Could Europa have liquid water?
questions.no_rag: Yes, scientists believe Europa has a salty liquid-water ocean under its icy crust, possibly twice the volume of Earth's oceans.
questions.no_rag_note: Plausible, but the "twice the volume" detail cannot be checked against the knowledge base.

claims.text: Very likely. The youth and smoothness of Europa's surface are attributed to a water ocean beneath the ice, which could conceivably harbor life.
The leading model is that heat from tidal flexing keeps the ocean liquid.
The Hubble Space Telescope has also detected water vapor plumes, similar to those seen on Enceladus.

questions.question: When was Mercury first explored?
questions.no_rag: Mercury was first explored by the Mariner 10 probe in 1974.
questions.no_rag_note: Silently picks one meaning of "Mercury" and never mentions the other.

claims.text: If you mean the planet, the first successful flyby was made by Mariner 10 in 1974.
If you mean NASA's Project Mercury, its first astronaut, Alan Shepard, flew a suborbital flight on May 5, 1961, shortly after Gagarin's orbit.

questions.question: Which Titan launched the Gemini astronauts?
questions.no_rag: The Gemini astronauts were launched on Titan II rockets.
questions.no_rag_note: Right but terse; the question is ambiguous for a retriever (Titan is also Saturn's moon).

claims.text: Gemini crews flew on the Titan II GLV, a modified intercontinental ballistic missile.
Titan rockets launched all Project Gemini crewed flights in the mid-1960s.

questions.question: What is the best pizza in Naples?
questions.no_rag: Many would point to L'Antica Pizzeria da Michele or Gino Sorbillo, both famous for classic Neapolitan margherita.
questions.no_rag_note: Answers confidently from memory. A RAG system scoped to space exploration should decline instead.

failure_cases.question: apollo-13
failure_cases.title: Chunks too small
failure_cases.lesson: With 48-token chunks every sentence is retrieved on its own. The top 3 fragments merely sound similar (one is about Apollo 11!) and the passages holding the evidence never reach the prompt. Lose the context around a fact and retrieval stops finding it.

failure_cases.question: mercury-ambiguous
failure_cases.title: Ambiguous question
failure_cases.lesson: "Mercury" is both a planet and a NASA programme. Watch the retrieval lines reach into two different regions of the map: the context mixes topics.

failure_cases.question: pizza
failure_cases.title: Out of corpus
failure_cases.lesson: Nothing in the corpus is about pizza. Every similarity is below the threshold, so the system declines. Set the threshold to 0: retrieval ALWAYS returns something, however irrelevant.

failure_cases.question: titan-gemini
failure_cases.title: Reranking to the rescue
failure_cases.lesson: Vector search confuses Titan the moon with Titan the rocket. The cross-encoder reads question and passage together and pushes the rocket passages to the top. Toggle reranking off to compare.
